title: Teaching
text:
Modules at Royal Holloway

International Political Economy
PR2500 · Second-year undergraduate module · Since 2017
The relationship between states and markets, power and wealth, in the world economy. The module introduces the main theories of international political economy and the history of its regimes and crises, then turns to trade, finance, production, labour, and development, and to current debates on race, gender, climate change, and global health.


Global Health Policy
PR3950 · Third-year undergraduate module · Since 2018
An introduction to global health policy, drawing on political economy, social epidemiology, and public health. The module examines the actors that make global health policy, from international organisations and governments to public-private partnerships, philanthropic foundations, and companies, and the health effects of inequality, trade, and austerity, as well as pandemics, universal health coverage, and climate change.

Prospective PhD students
I welcome enquiries from prospective PhD students working on the international financial institutions and global economic governance, social protection and global health policy, the political economy of climate change, or politics and development in Africa.
Royal Holloway asks applicants to secure a supervisor before they apply. If your project fits, please email me at thomas.stubbs@rhul.ac.uk with a short research proposal and your CV. The university’s Politics PhD page sets out the entry requirements and how to apply.

title: About
text:
Skip to main content
I am a social scientist working on international political economy, global health and development, and African politics. I am Professor of Global Political Economy in the Department of Politics and International Relations at Royal Holloway, University of London, where I have taught since 2017, and Research Associate in Political Economy at the Centre for Business Research, University of Cambridge. Before Royal Holloway, I was a lecturer in sociology at the University of Waikato in New Zealand and, before that, a research associate in sociology at the University of Cambridge, where I took my PhD.
Beyond the research described below, I write on African politics: on elections in Kenya, Rwanda, and Burundi, on ethnicity and the military in Kenya, and on conflict in the Sahel.

title: About
text:
Research
My research examines the international financial institutions, above all the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and how the global economy is governed. It follows two strands.

The IMF and its borrowers
What do IMF programmes do to the countries that take them? With Alexandros Kentikelenis and other colleagues, I have built a dataset of the policy conditions attached to IMF loans over four decades, drawn from the IMF’s own archives. With it, we study how conditionality is designed and how far governments comply with it, the IMF’s tax advice, and the effects of its programmes on social protection, health, inequality, state capacity, corruption, and protest. Our book A Thousand Cuts (Oxford University Press, 2023) brings this work together. It finds that although the content of IMF-mandated austerity has changed, the IMF still places a high burden of reform on its borrowers, and that these reforms reduce the availability of social services, widen income inequality, and harm population health.
The data are public on IMF Monitor, which I curate: a data hub used by academics, civil society, and policymakers to track activities of the International Monetary Fund.

Global economic governance: crisis finance, austerity, and climate
How is the global economy governed when a problem exceeds any one programme? My work here follows three questions. The first is crisis finance: how the global financial safety net of IMF resources, regional financing arrangements, and central bank swap lines responds to shocks such as Covid-19, and how far it reaches developing countries. The second is the wave of austerity that followed the pandemic, and what it costs public health. The third is climate change: how the IMF has brought the green transition into its surveillance, lending, and technical assistance, the subject of our book Greening the International Monetary Fund (Cambridge University Press, 2025) and of a series of reports for Recourse Foundation. A Philip Leverhulme Prize, for 2027–28, will support the next stage of this work, on the social consequences of global economic governance.

title: Books
text:
Skip to main content








Greening the International Monetary FundWith Alexandros Kentikelenis · 2025 · Cambridge University Press · Elements in Organizational Response to Climate Change Open access PDF DOI Replication data
The IMF has emerged as a key player in climate policy, and this closer engagement with the economic dimensions of climate change holds the promise of helping countries preempt large-scale economic dislocations from climate risks. But how much progress has the IMF made in supporting the green transition and what is the policy track record of its climate loans and policy advice? Based on extensive new evidence, Greening the International Monetary Fund points to the multifaceted, and at times contradictory, ways green transition objectives have become embedded within IMF activities.





A Thousand Cuts: Social Protection in the Age of AusterityWith Alexandros Kentikelenis · 2023 · Oxford University Press DOI Replication data
A Thousand Cuts: Social Protection in the Age of Austerity provides a comprehensive analysis of IMF policies around the world. Based on novel data from the IMF archives, the book offers a replicable database of all IMF-mandated reforms from 1980–2019, and examines their effects on social policies and outcomes. The analysis reveals that although the precise content of IMF-mandated austerity has changed, the organisation continues to place a high burden of reform on its borrowers. These reforms decrease the availability of important social services and contribute to rises in income inequality and declines in population health.


Praise


“A Thousand Cuts is the most significant piece of research on austerity’s pernicious effects in the Global South. Alexandros Kentikelenis and Thomas Stubbs meticulously demonstrate that budget cuts fail poorer countries time and time again. This is essential reading for anyone concerned with how the world can avoid economic mistakes of the past, and how governments can implement policies that promote social protection.”
Mark Blyth, The William R. Rhodes ’57 Professor of International Economics, Brown University


“This carefully researched book examines more than 6,000 IMF loan documents over four decades to show convincingly that IMF conditionalities still require regressive public policies that in turn have regressive socio-economic outcomes. Such an important book must be read carefully in every national capital, and most of all in Washington, D.C. It forms the basis for arguments for major change if the IMF is to be fit for purpose in the contemporary world economy.”
Jayati Ghosh, Professor of Economics, University of Massachusetts Amherst


“In brilliant, novel detail, A Thousand Cuts provides a devastating indictment of the IMF’s austerity-driven conditionality and its systemic undermining of social policies and outcomes. It should be required reading not just for scholars and policy activists, but also for IMF staff intent on substantively changing the institution’s practices.”
Daniela Gabor, Professor of Economics, School of Oriental and African Studies


“A Thousand Cuts is the first comprehensive, data-driven analysis of the outcomes of IMF lending policies. While the methodology is rigorous and writing style elegant, the conclusions are not pretty. Kentikelenis and Stubbs document the consistently devastating social consequences of ill-conceived austerity measures by the IMF. This truly original and alarming new volume is mandatory reading for anyone interested in how to build a more progressive global economic governance based on evidence over ideology.”
Kevin P. Gallagher, Director of the Global Development Policy Center, Boston University
